120.title: Pentecost and ordinary time
120.hook: after Pentecost comes the long green season, when faith gets lived in the ordinary
120.howItsDone: Many churches celebrate Pentecost in red, fifty days after Easter, remembering the gift of the Spirit; then comes ordinary time, the long green season of numbered Sundays when the Gospels are read week by week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascha, and your line: he is risen indeed. Did you carry some good news to someone? Easter runs fifty days. Today, day fifty, and then the longest season of all. Day one hundred twenty.

Jerusalem again, seven weeks after Easter. The city is full of pilgrims for a Jewish harvest feast, visitors from all over the known world. The book of Acts says: "And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place." Jesus's followers, together in a house. Then a sound like a rushing wind fills the place, and something like flames rests on each of them. They pour out into the street talking, and the crowd, people from Egypt, Rome, Arabia, Asia, each hears them in their own language. Some are amazed. Others laugh and say they're drunk, at nine in the morning. It's loud, bright and red. And then the church calendar does something surprising. It turns green, and goes quiet, for months. Today's word is that long quiet.
screen: `SEVEN WEEKS AFTER EASTER.` → `WIND AND FIRE.` → `EVERY LANGUAGE, THEN GREEN.`

segments.voice: Start with Pentecost. It's Greek for fiftieth. It was a Jewish feast first, Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, and Jews still keep it. Christians remember it as the day the Holy Spirit came, and many call it the birthday of the church. Churches wear red for the fire. Then comes ordinary time. And here's the surprise in the name. Ordinary doesn't mean boring. It comes from the Latin for numbered, like ordinal numbers: the Sundays are simply counted, one after another, the tenth, the eleventh, the twelfth. In some churches they're called the Sundays after Pentecost, or after Trinity. The color is green, the color of things growing. And it's the longest season of the year, stretching from late spring through summer and fall, about half the calendar. No big feasts. No fasting. Just week after week of the Gospels read in order, and life lived. That's the point. After all the drama of the circle, the waiting and the birth, the desert and the cross and the empty tomb and the fire, the church year says: now go and live it on a Tuesday. Paul wrote: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord." In the 1600s, a Carmelite brother named Lawrence worked in his monastery's kitchen, and said he felt as near to God among the pots and pans as at the altar. So ends our twelve days on the circle of the year: from Advent's candles to the long green season. The holy days point back to the ordinary ones.
screen: `PENTECOST: THE FIFTIETH DAY.` · `ORDINARY MEANS NUMBERED.` · `GREEN, AND HALF THE YEAR.` · `GOD AMONG THE POTS AND PANS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one ordinary task. Settle, and breathe. Choose something you'll do today anyway. Washing dishes. Folding laundry. Walking to the car. Answering email. Picture yourself doing it slowly, with full attention, as if it mattered. If you pray, you can offer it to God before you start, and do it as prayer. If you don't, do it as an act of care, for the people it serves. Then let the rest of the time be quiet. The bell holds the time.
Ordinary time. The long green season of the church year. Ordinary meaning numbered, not boring: faith lived week by week. Today's word.
Your line: the ordinary is holy. Today, do one ordinary task slowly, as if it were a prayer. Tomorrow, a new stretch: sabbath and scripture. Day one hundred twenty.

Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover. Jews still keep it.
ordinary time is the shortest season
it's the longest, about half the year, in green.

what it means: the long green season after Pentecost, when faith is lived week by week in everyday life.

121.title: God rested (Genesis 2:1–3)
121.hook: on the seventh day God stopped and blessed the stopping
121.howItsDone: Christians read the seventh day of creation as the root of the sabbath and of their own day of rest; churches and families set aside a weekly day for worship and rest, and Jews keep Shabbat from Friday sundown to Saturday sundown.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecost and ordinary time, and your line: the ordinary is holy. Did a chore turn into something more? That closed the circle of the year. Now ten days on sabbath and scripture. Day one hundred twenty-one.

When did you last stop? Not switch tasks. Not scroll on the couch while half-answering messages. Actually stop, with nothing left running. For some, the honest answer is: I can't remember. There's always one more email, one more load of laundry, one more thing. Now turn to the opening of the Bible. Six days of making: light, sky, sea, land, stars, fish, birds, animals, people. Every day, something new. And then the seventh day comes, and the story says God does something that sounds almost strange for God. Nothing. On purpose. Today, the Bible's seventh day.
screen: `WHEN DID YOU LAST STOP?` → `SIX DAYS OF MAKING.` → `THEN, ON PURPOSE, NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the text, in the King James Bible: "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it." The Hebrew word for rested is shavat. It means to stop, to cease. And the word sabbath, shabbat, is linked to it: the stopping. Notice: God doesn't rest because he's tired. Isaiah says God "fainteth not, neither is weary." The rest isn't recovery. It's a choice. The work is good, and finished, and so it's time to stop and enjoy it. Then something even stranger. God blesses the stopping. He makes the seventh day holy. The Jewish thinker Abraham Joshua Heschel pointed out that the first thing in the Bible God calls holy isn't a mountain or a temple. It's a day. A piece of time. Later, the commandment comes: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." And in Deuteronomy, it gets a second reason: you were once slaves in Egypt. Slaves can't stop. So rest is freedom, and it's for everyone in the house: children, workers, strangers, even the animals. Jews keep that day from Friday sundown to Saturday sundown, with candles, a meal and rest. Christians share this first page with them, and tomorrow we'll see how Christians came to keep their own day. But it all starts here: before any command to rest, God rests first, and calls it blessed.
screen: `SHAVAT: TO STOP.` · `NOT TIRED. FINISHED.` · `THE FIRST HOLY THING IS A DAY.` · `REST IS FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop completely. Let your hands go still in your lap, palms open, once the bell starts. Settle, and breathe. Don't plan. Don't fix. Don't review your list. If a task comes to mind, tell it: later. Just be here, doing nothing, on purpose. It may feel uncomfortable at first, even guilty. Let it. If you pray, you can rest in God for these moments. If you don't, simply rest. Later today, stop again, for five whole minutes. The bell holds the time.
God rested. On the seventh day God stopped, and blessed the stopping, and made the day holy. Today's word.
Your line: rest is blessed. Today, when one task ends, stop completely for five minutes before you start the next. Day one hundred twenty-one.

122.title: Why Sunday
122.hook: most Christians gather on Sunday, the day of the resurrection; Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday
122.carry: the first day, a new start
122.howItsDone: Christians gather for worship on Sunday, the day of the resurrection, and some keep it as a day of rest; Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists worship and rest on Saturday, the seventh day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, God rested on the seventh day, and your line: rest is blessed. Did you manage five minutes of stopping? The seventh day is Saturday. So why do churches meet on Sunday? Day one hundred twenty-two.

A town called Troas, on the coast of what's now Turkey. It's evening, the first day of the week, and a group of Christians is crammed into an upstairs room lit with oil lamps. The book of Acts says: "And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them." And Paul keeps going. Until midnight. A young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window, gets sleepier and sleepier, and falls from the third story to the ground. Paul runs down, wraps his arms around him, and says, he's alive. Then everyone goes back upstairs, eats, and keeps talking until dawn. It's a scare with a happy ending. And it quietly shows something: Christians were already gathering on the first day of the week. Today's word is its name.
screen: `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM IN TROAS.` → `PAUL PREACHES TILL MIDNIGHT.` → `THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.`

segments.voice: The Lord's Day. Why the first day? Because all four Gospels say the tomb was found empty on it. John begins: "The first day of the week cometh Mary Magdalene early, when it was yet dark, unto the sepulchre." Sunday morning. So early Christians gave that day a new name. In Revelation, John says, "I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day." In Greek, kyriake, the Lord's. And the name stuck. In modern Greek, Sunday is still Kyriaki. In Spanish it's domingo, in Italian domenica, both from the Latin for the Lord's. And in Russian, the word for Sunday simply means resurrection. Some early Christian writers called Sunday the eighth day. The week of creation ends on the seventh; the resurrection starts a new creation, a new first day. So for them, Sunday isn't the sabbath moved over by one. It's a new start. Later, the emperor Constantine made Sunday a legal day of rest in the Roman Empire. Not all Christians keep Sunday. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists worship on Saturday, because the commandment names the seventh day, and they keep it as written. For Catholics and Orthodox Christians, Sunday worship is expected of the faithful; Protestant churches gather on it too. The day differs. The idea underneath is shared: one day, set apart.
screen: `THE TOMB, ON THE FIRST DAY.` · `KYRIAKE: THE LORD'S.` · `THE EIGHTH DAY, A NEW CREATION.` · `SOME KEEP THE SEVENTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your hour. Settle, and breathe. Look ahead at the coming week. Where is there one hour you could set apart? Sunday morning, Saturday afternoon, a weekday evening. Picture it. What would you do with it? Not chores. Not errands. Something that restores you: worship, a walk, a long meal, a nap, time with someone you love. If you pray, you can offer that hour to God ahead of time. If you don't, simply promise it to yourself. Then rest for what's left of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Lord's Day. The Christian name for Sunday, the day of the resurrection, the first day of the week. Today's word.
Your line: the first day, a new start. Today, put one restful hour in your calendar this week, and guard it. Day one hundred twenty-two.

123.title: Made for you (Mark 2:27)
123.hook: the sabbath was made for people, not people for the sabbath
123.carry: rest is a gift, not a test
123.howItsDone: Christians often quote Mark 2:27 when they talk about rest: some keep Sunday as a day of worship and rest while treating acts of mercy and real need as fitting on that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord's Day, and your line: the first day, a new start. Did you find a restful hour in your week? Today, what that hour is for. Day one hundred twenty-three.

Have you ever taken a day off and spent it feeling guilty? Lying on the couch, but running through everything you should be doing. Resting badly. Resting like it's a test you might fail. Now, a grainfield on a sabbath. Jesus and his disciples are walking along a path between the rows of grain. The disciples are hungry. As they walk, they pull off heads of grain, rub them in their hands, and eat. Some Pharisees, teachers who took the sabbath very seriously, see it and object. To them, picking grain is harvesting, harvesting is work, and work isn't allowed today. It's a real question, asked by people who cared about the sabbath. Jesus answers with a short, sharp line. Today's word is its heart.
screen: `RESTING LIKE IT'S A TEST.` → `A GRAINFIELD ON THE SABBATH.` → `IS PICKING GRAIN WORK?`

segments.voice: First, Jesus reminds them of a story they all knew. Once, David and his hungry men were given holy bread from the house of God, bread only priests were meant to eat. Human need came first. Then he says it, in the King James words: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Made for you. Christians hear in it that the sabbath is a gift, given to people, to feed them and free them, not a trap, or a test they could fail. And he adds, "Therefore the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath," a claim Christians take as a statement of who Jesus is. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say the sabbath doesn't matter, or that rest is optional. He says what it's for. It's worth being fair to the Pharisees here. They weren't villains. They were trying to protect something holy, and Jewish teachers debated carefully what counted as work. Later rabbis, heirs of that conversation, taught that saving a life overrides the sabbath, and one rabbinic commentary on Exodus has a saying remarkably close to this one: the sabbath is given to you, not you to the sabbath. So this is a conversation inside a shared love of the day. For Christians today, the line cuts both ways. For people who keep strict rules about Sunday, it's a reminder that rest is for people's good. And for people who can't rest at all, who feel guilty on the couch, it's a permission slip. In this reading, rest isn't something earned. It's something given.
screen: `DAVID AND THE HOLY BREAD.` · `MADE FOR MAN, NOT MAN FOR IT.` · `NOT VILLAINS: A SHARED LOVE.` · `A GIFT, NOT A TEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest without earning it. Settle, and breathe. Let your body get heavy. Now listen for the voice that says you haven't done enough to deserve this. When it speaks, don't argue. Just answer it quietly: this was made for me. If you pray, you can receive this rest as a gift from God. If you don't, receive it anyway, as a gift from the day. Nothing to accomplish. Nothing to pass. The bell holds the time.
Made for you. The sabbath was made for people, not people for the sabbath: rest is a gift given for our good. Today's word.
Your line: rest is a gift, not a test. Today, rest for ten minutes without guilt, and when the guilty voice starts, tell it: made for me. Day one hundred twenty-three.

124.title: A small sabbath
124.hook: a phone off, a walk, a meal with no hurry: sabbath can start small
124.howItsDone: Alongside or instead of a full day of rest, some Christians keep small sabbaths: an hour of quiet, a screen-free meal, a Sunday afternoon without errands, or a daily walk for prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sabbath was made for you, and your line: rest is a gift, not a test. Did you answer the guilty voice? Today, for everyone who's thinking: a whole day off? Not in my life. Day one hundred twenty-four.
screen: `REST IS A GIFT, NOT A TEST.`

segments.voice: Maybe a whole day of rest sounds lovely and impossible. You work weekends. You have small kids who don't know what a sabbath is. You have two jobs, or a parent who needs you, or a phone that never stops. Here's a scene for you. Jesus's disciples have just come back from traveling and teaching, full of stories, worn out. And so many people are crowding around, Mark says, that they don't even have time to eat. Jesus looks at them and says, in the King James words: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." Not forever. Not a month-long retreat. A while. So they get into a boat and head for somewhere quiet. Today's word is a sabbath sized for real life.
screen: `A WHOLE DAY? NOT IN MY LIFE.` → `NO TIME EVEN TO EAT.` → `REST A WHILE.`

segments.voice: A small sabbath. The full sabbath is a whole day, and those who keep it, Jewish and Christian, treasure it. But sabbath can also start small. An hour with the phone in a drawer. A walk with nowhere to get to. A meal where nobody hurries. What makes it sabbath isn't the length. It's the stopping. And here's the honest part of Mark's story. They get in the boat, and the crowd sees where they're going and runs around the lake to meet them. By the time they land, a huge crowd is waiting. Jesus has compassion on them, and teaches them. So the rest was short, and interrupted. It still counted. The Gospels show Jesus slipping away more than once, early in the morning or up a mountain, to be alone and pray. Luke says: "And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed." Short withdrawals, in the middle of a crowded life. And in Matthew he says: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." Christians today practice small sabbaths in all kinds of ways. A Sunday afternoon with no shopping. A candle lit at dinner. Screens off after nine. A daily walk without headphones. None of these would satisfy a strict sabbath keeper, and they're not meant to replace a full day for those who keep one. They're a door. Often the hard part isn't finding the hour. It's actually putting the phone down.
screen: `SABBATH CAN START SMALL.` · `THE REST WAS SHORT, AND COUNTED.` · `HE WITHDREW, AND PRAYED.` · `I WILL GIVE YOU REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put the phone down, now. If you're listening on it, set it face down, or across the room, and let the bell find you. Settle, and breathe. Notice the pull to check it. Just notice. Let it pass. If you pray, you can say his words to his friends quietly: rest a while. If you don't, just rest a while. Before the bell ends, choose one hour later today or tomorrow when the phone goes in a drawer. The bell holds the time.
A small sabbath. A short, real stop in a busy life: an hour, a walk, a meal. The stopping is what makes it holy. Today's word.
Your line: stop. it still counts. Today, put your phone away for one full hour, and if the hour gets interrupted, remember the boat. Day one hundred twenty-four.

screen: `DAY 124 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A LIBRARY, NOT A BOOK.`

125.title: A library, not a book
125.hook: Protestants have 66 books, Catholics 73, Orthodox a few more
125.howItsDone: Protestant Bibles contain sixty-six books, Catholic Bibles seventy-three and Orthodox Bibles a few more; all share the same twenty-seven books of the New Testament, and many study Bibles explain the differences in their introductions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a small sabbath, and your line: stop. it still counts. Did your phone spend an hour in a drawer? Now, the second half of this stretch: scripture. Day one hundred twenty-five.

Pick up a Bible. It looks like one book: one cover, one spine, thin pages, tiny print. Now open it to the contents page. Genesis. Exodus. Psalms. Proverbs. Isaiah. Matthew. Romans. Revelation. Dozens of titles. Written over more than a thousand years, by many different hands, in three languages: Hebrew, a little Aramaic, and Greek. Some of it is poetry. Some is law. Some is history, some letters, some songs, some wild visions of the end of the world. It isn't a book at all. It's a library. Even the word Bible says so. It comes from the Greek ta biblia: the books. Plural. And here's a question almost nobody asks until they compare two Bibles side by side: who decided which books go in? Today's word is the answer.
screen: `ONE COVER, DOZENS OF TITLES.` → `THREE LANGUAGES, A THOUSAND YEARS.` → `TA BIBLIA: THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Canon. From the Greek kanon, a straight reed, a measuring rod, a rule. The canon is the list of books a church measures as scripture. And the lists aren't all the same. Protestant Bibles have sixty-six books: thirty-nine in the Old Testament, twenty-seven in the New. Catholic Bibles have seventy-three, adding seven books to the Old Testament, among them Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, and the two books of Maccabees, plus extra parts of Esther and Daniel. Catholics call these deuterocanonical, the second canon; Protestants often call them the Apocrypha. Orthodox Bibles have a few more still, such as a third book of Maccabees and a Psalm 151. And the Ethiopian Orthodox Church has the broadest canon of all, including the book of Enoch. Here's a surprise: the King James Bible of 1611 printed the Apocrypha, between the two testaments. Many later printings left it out. What almost everyone shares is the New Testament: the same twenty-seven books, in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles alike. The earliest list that matches those twenty-seven exactly comes from a bishop named Athanasius, in a letter from the year 367. And the Jewish Bible, the Tanakh, has the same books as the Protestant Old Testament, arranged in a different order and counted as twenty-four. Christians hold these differences without pretending they don't exist. But they tend to agree on what the library is for. The writers disagree, argue, grieve and sing, and Christians hear them all telling one long story: God and people, from a garden to a city. The book itself says, "All scripture is given by inspiration of God."
screen: `KANON: A MEASURING ROD.` · `66, 73, AND A FEW MORE.` · `THE SAME 27 IN THE NEW.` · `MANY VOICES, ONE STORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk the shelves. If there's a Bible near you, open it to the contents page. If not, picture a long bookshelf. Settle, and breathe. Let the titles go by slowly: stories at the start, then laws, then histories, then songs and wisdom, then prophets, then four Gospels, letters, and a vision at the end. Notice one title you've never read, or never heard of. Just let it catch your eye. If you pray, you can ask for curiosity. If you don't, simply notice what you're curious about. The bell holds the time.
Canon. From the Greek for measuring rod. The list of books a church accepts as scripture. Today's word.
Your line: many voices, one story. Today, look up the one book you noticed, and read just its first few lines. Day one hundred twenty-five.

126.title: Two testaments
126.hook: Christians read the Hebrew scriptures as the first part of their own story
126.howItsDone: Christians read both testaments in worship, often an Old Testament reading, a psalm, a New Testament letter and a Gospel on the same Sunday; some call the first part the Hebrew Bible or First Testament out of respect.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the canon, and your line: many voices, one story. This week: Pentecost's fire, God resting, Sunday, a sabbath made for you, a small sabbath, a library. Eighteen weeks on the path. Today, the library's two halves. Day one hundred twenty-six.

A sabbath day in the synagogue at Nazareth. Jesus, a local man, stands up to read. Someone hands him a scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He unrolls it, finds a passage about good news for the poor and freedom for captives, reads it aloud, rolls it back up, and sits down. Every eye in the room is on him. Now look at what he was holding. Not a New Testament. There wasn't one yet. None of it had been written. The scriptures Jesus read, quoted, prayed and argued from were the Hebrew scriptures. When the Gospels speak of "the scriptures," this is what they mean. So how did the Christian Bible end up in two halves, one called old and one called new? Today's word is the name of each half.
screen: `A SCROLL OF ISAIAH.` → `THERE WAS NO NEW TESTAMENT YET.` → `TWO HALVES: OLD AND NEW.`

segments.voice: Testament. It comes from the Latin testamentum, which translates a Greek word, diatheke: covenant. A binding agreement. So Old Testament and New Testament really mean old covenant and new covenant. And the phrase new covenant comes from the Hebrew scriptures themselves. The prophet Jeremiah says: "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah." Centuries later, at the Last Supper, Jesus picks up a cup, and in the King James words says: "This cup is the new testament in my blood." That's where the name comes from. Now, the word old. It can sound like outdated, used up. That's not how the church has held it. Early on, a teacher named Marcion wanted to throw out the Hebrew scriptures entirely. The church said no, and kept both. For Christians, the first testament isn't a warm-up act. It's the first part of their own story: creation, Abraham, the exodus, David, the psalms, the prophets. Jesus lived inside that story. Out of respect, some Christians and scholars also say the Hebrew Bible, or the First Testament. And it's worth saying plainly: Jews read these same scriptures, the Tanakh, as complete in themselves, not as the first half of anything. Christians read them as leading to Jesus. Both communities hold them sacred, and read them in their own ways. For Christians, the carry is simple: the story began long before Bethlehem.
screen: `TESTAMENT: COVENANT.` · `JEREMIAH: A NEW COVENANT.` · `THE CUP AT THE LAST SUPPER.` · `NOT A WARM-UP ACT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the first psalm. If you have a Bible, open it to Psalm 1. It's only six verses. If you don't, listen to one line of it: "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season." Settle, and breathe. Let the picture come: a tree by a river, roots deep, in no hurry. Jews and Christians both pray the psalms. If you pray, you can pray the line. If you don't, stay with the tree. The bell holds the time.
screen: `LIKE A TREE PLANTED BY THE RIVERS OF WATER.`
